slides.title: Model Compression: From Lab-Sized to Edge-Ready
slides.notes: Today, we're not just talking about making models smaller. We're talking about making them smarter, faster, and ready for the real world.

slides.title: The Core Challenge: Model Bloat is a Real-World Bottleneck
points: Real-time applications demand low latency (e.g., <100ms).
Edge devices have tight constraints on memory and power.
Cloud costs scale with model size and compute time.
The result: a great model in the lab can be a failure in production.

slides.title: The Optimization Toolbox: A Spectrum of Choices
points: We can think of compression techniques on a spectrum:
Easy & Fast (but less effective): Post-Training Methods
Complex & Slow (but more powerful): In-Training Methods
This project is a journey across that spectrum.

slides.title: Our Mission: From a Bloated Baseline to an Edge-Ready Model
points: Starting Point: A 14MB MobileNetV2 model.
Goal: A model under 4MB with less than 100ms latency on a CPU.
Constraint: Minimize accuracy loss as much as possible.

slides.title: Deconstructing the Baseline: Why MobileNetV2?
points: It's not just a random choice. It's designed for efficiency.
Key features: Inverted residuals and linear bottlenecks.
This architecture gives us a head start in optimization.

slides.title: Profiling the Baseline: Where Does the Time Go?
points: Insight: Before you optimize, you must profile.
We found that the majority of latency was in the early convolutional layers.
This tells us where to focus our optimization efforts.

slides.title: The Dataset's Quirks: Not Your Average Benchmark
points: The household items dataset has its own challenges:
Fine-grained distinctions (e.g., different types of chairs).
Variable lighting and backgrounds.
This makes preserving accuracy even more challenging.

slides.title: Baseline Performance: Our North Star
points: Accuracy: 92%
Size: 14.1 MB
Latency: 250ms (on our target CPU)
This is the benchmark we have to beat.

slides.title: First Strike: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)
points: The fastest and easiest way to get a win.
We converted the model from FP32 to INT8.
The key insight here is the 'calibration' step.

slides.title: PTQ Deep Dive: The Crucial Role of Calibration
points: Insight: The quality of your calibration data determines the quality of your quantized model.
A small, but representative, dataset is needed to determine the quantization parameters.
Using bad calibration data can lead to a huge drop in accuracy.

slides.title: PTQ Results: The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly
points: The Good: Model size dropped to 3.6 MB (a 4x improvement!).
The Bad: Latency improved to 150ms.
The Ugly: Accuracy fell to 85% (a 7% drop). Unacceptable.

slides.title: Next Up: Post-Training Pruning
points: Let's try removing some of the model's connections.
We used magnitude-based unstructured pruning.
The key trade-off here is sparsity vs. accuracy.

slides.title: Pruning Deep Dive: The 'Sparsity Tax'
points: Insight: Accuracy doesn't drop linearly with sparsity.
There's a tipping point where the model collapses.
We found this point to be around 60% sparsity for our model.

slides.title: The 'Aha!' Moment of Post-Training
points: Insight: PTQ and pruning don't always compose well.
Pruning changes the weight distribution, which can invalidate the calibration data used for PTQ.
This is a key reason why post-training methods have a ceiling.

slides.title: Post-Training Verdict: A Good Start, But We Need More
points: Pros: Fast, easy to implement, good for initial results.
Cons: Significant accuracy loss, limited compression potential.
Conclusion: We need to bring out the heavy artillery.

slides.title: Leveling Up: In-Training Optimization
points: By integrating compression into the training loop, we can recover lost accuracy.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's more complex, but the results are worth it.

slides.title: Quantization-Aware Training (QAT): Training for a Low-Precision World
points: QAT simulates quantization during training.
This allows the model to adapt its weights to be more robust to quantization errors.
The key mechanism is the 'fake quantization' node.

slides.title: QAT Deep Dive: The Power of 'Fake' Quantization
points: Insight: By simulating the quantization process in the forward pass, we can use standard backpropagation to train the model.
The model learns to keep its weights within the quantizable range.
This is a powerful and elegant solution to the accuracy loss problem.

slides.title: QAT vs. PTQ: A Tale of Two Quantizations
points: PTQ: 85% accuracy.
QAT: 91.5% accuracy!
Insight: QAT clawed back almost all of the accuracy lost by PTQ.
This is a huge win and a key takeaway of the project.

slides.title: Pruning-in-Training: A More 'Gentle' Approach
points: Instead of ripping out weights at the end, we gradually remove them during training.
This gives the model time to heal and re-learn.
The key here is the 'pruning schedule'.

slides.title: Pruning Deep Dive: The Importance of the Pruning Schedule
points: Insight: A gradual pruning schedule (e.g., from 0% to 50% sparsity over 10 epochs) yields much better results than one-shot pruning.
This is because it gives the model a chance to adapt.
We found an aggressive schedule hurt accuracy significantly.

slides.title: Knowledge Distillation: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants
points: A fascinating technique where a smaller 'student' model learns from a larger 'teacher' model.
The student learns not just the correct labels, but the teacher's reasoning.
This is captured in the 'soft labels'.

slides.title: KD Deep Dive: The 'Dark Knowledge' in Soft Labels
points: Insight: The teacher's soft labels (e.g., 90% cat, 10% dog) provide much more information than a one-hot label (100% cat).
This 'dark knowledge' helps the student to generalize better.
It's a powerful form of regularization.

slides.title: The 'Synergy' Insight: Combining In-Training Techniques
points: Insight: These techniques are not mutually exclusive. They can be combined for even greater effect.
For example, we can use KD to train a model that is being pruned and quantized at the same time.
This is the core idea behind our pipeline.

slides.title: In-Training Verdict: The Path to Production-Ready Models
points: Pros: High accuracy, high compression ratios.
Cons: Complex, time-consuming, requires careful tuning.
Conclusion: This is the way to build state-of-the-art, optimized models.

slides.title: From Techniques to a Pipeline: The Order Matters!
points: Insight: The order in which you apply these techniques is a critical design decision.
Prune then Quantize? Or Quantize then Prune?
We found that pruning first, then applying QAT and KD, gave the best results.

slides.title: Our Multi-Stage Pipeline: A Deliberate Design
points: Stage 1: Pruning-in-Training to 50% sparsity.
Stage 2: Quantization-Aware Training on the pruned model.
Stage 3: Knowledge Distillation as a final fine-tuning step.
This pipeline is designed to maximize compression while preserving accuracy.

slides.title: Pipeline Stage 1: Pruning - The 'Sculpting' Phase
points: We carefully removed 50% of the model's weights over several epochs.
This gave us a smaller, more efficient model to work with in the next stages.

slides.title: Pipeline Stage 2: QAT - The 'Refining' Phase
points: We took the pruned model and made it aware of the quantization process.
This was the most critical step for recovering accuracy.

slides.title: Pipeline Stage 3: KD - The 'Polishing' Phase
points: Finally, we used the original baseline model as a teacher to give our student model a final accuracy boost.
This helped it to generalize even better.

slides.title: The 'Eureka!' Moment of the Pipeline
points: Insight: The combination of QAT and KD was incredibly powerful.
QAT recovered the accuracy lost to quantization, and KD pushed it even further.
This synergy was the key to the success of the project.

slides.title: The Final Model: Lean, Mean, and Accurate
points: Accuracy: 91.8%
Size: 3.6 MB
Latency: 95ms
We achieved our goals!

slides.title: Deployment: The Final Frontier
points: A great model is useless if you can't deploy it.
We deployed our final model as a serverless API on Google Cloud Run.
This makes it easy to integrate into any application.

slides.title: Why Cloud Run? The 'Serverless' Advantage
points: Insight: Serverless is a great fit for ML deployment.
Pay-per-use: You only pay when your model is being used.
Auto-scaling: It can handle traffic spikes without any manual intervention.
Easy to manage: No servers to provision or maintain.

slides.title: The Deployment Workflow: Docker, Flask, and GCP
points: 1. We wrapped our model in a simple Flask API.
2. We containerized the application using Docker.
3. We pushed the container to Google Container Registry.
4. We deployed the container to Cloud Run with a single command.

slides.title: The 'Gotcha' of Deployment: The Cold Start Problem
points: Insight: Serverless has a dark side - the cold start.
If your model isn't being used, it can be scaled down to zero.
The first request after a scale-down can be very slow.
Solution: Configure a minimum number of instances to keep warm.

slides.title: The Final Showdown: Baseline vs. Compressed
slides.notes: A powerful visual comparing the two models side-by-side on size, latency, and accuracy.

slides.title: The Business Impact: From Tech Specs to Business Value
points: Insight: What does this mean in the real world?
Reduced cloud costs by 75% due to smaller size and faster inference.
Improved user experience by reducing latency by 62%.
This is how you justify the engineering effort.

slides.title: Key Takeaways & 'Rules of Thumb' for Model Optimization
points: 1. Always profile your model first.
2. Start with post-training quantization for a quick win.
3. Use QAT to recover accuracy.
4. A multi-stage pipeline is the key to state-of-the-art results.
5. Don't forget about the business impact.

slides.title: Q&A
slides.notes: Thank you. I hope this has given you a deeper insight into the art and science of model optimization.
